questions.q: A company shares 5 TB datasets stored in a private S3 bucket with partners worldwide. Downloads must be fast and the bucket must accept requests only from CloudFront. What should the team configure?

options.t: A CloudFront distribution with Origin Access Control and a bucket policy for the `cloudfront.amazonaws.com` principal
options.why: Right: OAC signs requests to S3 and the policy limits access to the distribution through `AWS:SourceArn`.

options.t: A public bucket with a CloudFront distribution using the S3 website endpoint
options.why: Wrong: the bucket stays public, so people can bypass CloudFront.

options.t: S3 Transfer Acceleration on the bucket
options.why: Wrong: it speeds up uploads to S3 and does not cache downloads at the edge.

options.t: Global Accelerator in front of the bucket
options.why: Wrong: it does not cache content and is for TCP/UDP traffic with fixed IPs.

questions.explain: Private S3 + CloudFront means OAC plus a bucket policy tied to the distribution ARN.
questions.remember: Private S3 content through CloudFront → OAC (not OAI, not a public bucket) and a bucket policy with principal cloudfront.amazonaws.com and AWS:SourceArn.
variants: The origin is an S3 static website endpoint → it is a custom origin, so OAC does not work.
Objects are SSE-KMS → also allow the CloudFront service principal in the KMS key policy.
The legacy method is OAI → still works but OAC is recommended.

questions.q: Paying subscribers must download a single report for one hour only. An application authorizes each user first. Which approach fits?

options.t: The app returns a CloudFront signed URL with a one-hour expiry, signed with a key group private key
options.why: Right: a signed URL gives time-limited access to a single object.
Wrong: cookies fit many files, such as a video library, not one report.
Wrong: it filters by country, not by user or time.
Wrong: it protects form fields, not downloads.

questions.explain: One object, limited time → signed URL.
questions.remember: One file with expiry → signed URL; many files (video, whole area) → signed cookies. Use key groups, not root key pairs.
variants: A whole video library needs auth → signed cookies.
Direct S3 access, including uploads, without a distribution → S3 presigned URL.
The behavior must have Restrict viewer access enabled with a trusted key group.

questions.q: Hundreds of edge locations all request the same large objects from a limited-capacity origin on a cache miss. Which feature lowers the load on the origin the most?

options.why: Right: an extra caching layer in one Region collapses misses from all edges into one request to the origin.
Wrong: it limits edge locations for cost and does not reduce misses.
Wrong: it is unrelated to origin load.
Wrong: it blocks countries and does not collapse requests.

questions.explain: Origin Shield collapses misses from many edges.
questions.remember: Many edges hitting one origin with the same misses → Origin Shield (higher hit ratio, adds a per-request fee).
variants: Poor hit ratio from a wide cache key → shrink the cache key first.
The origin is fine but cost is high in far Regions → price class.
Origin down → origin group failover.

questions.q: A CloudFront distribution in front of an ALB has a poor cache hit ratio. The cache policy forwards all cookies and all query strings. What should the engineer do?

options.t: Include only the needed headers, cookies and query strings in the cache key, and lengthen TTLs
options.why: Right: a smaller cache key fragments the cache less.
Wrong: invalidations remove cached objects and lower the hit ratio further.
Wrong: it turns caching off.
Wrong: that protects against abuse and does not improve the hit ratio.

questions.explain: Fewer elements in the cache key → higher hit ratio.
questions.remember: Low hit ratio → reduce cache key elements, normalize query strings, lengthen TTL, use versioned names. Things forwarded but not keyed go in an origin request policy.
variants: Values needed by the origin but not by the cache → origin request policy.
API with no caching wanted → CachingDisabled.
Static S3 content → CachingOptimized.

questions.q: A team must serve new static assets right after each release without relying on invalidations, and wants to keep long TTLs. What is the best approach?

options.why: Right: each release is a new cache key, so old objects never need removal.

options.t: Run `/*` invalidation after every release only
options.why: Wrong: it works, but it costs after the first 1,000 paths a month and is not the preferred way.
Wrong: this removes the benefit of caching.

options.t: Use Lambda@Edge to rewrite every response
options.why: Wrong: it adds cost and latency and is not needed.

questions.remember: Instant new asset version with long TTL → version the file names; invalidation is the fallback (first 1,000 paths a month free).
variants: A single file must disappear now → invalidate that path.
HTML entry page needs fresh content → short TTL for it.
Cache hit ratio matters → keep long TTLs on versioned assets.

questions.q: A data team exposes an internal Superset dashboard. The ALB must have no public IP, yet users reach it through CloudFront with WAF. What should they use?

options.t: A CloudFront VPC origin pointing to the ALB in a private subnet
options.why: Right: CloudFront connects privately, so the ALB has no public exposure.

options.t: An internet-facing ALB with a public security group
options.why: Wrong: it leaves the ALB exposed to direct access.
Wrong: that is for static website content.
Wrong: it is a caching layer and does not make the origin private.

questions.explain: VPC origins keep private ALB/NLB/EC2 origins private.
questions.remember: Origin must have no public exposure → CloudFront VPC origin. Without VPC origins → SG allowing the CloudFront managed prefix list plus a secret header.
variants: Public ALB that must only accept CloudFront → prefix list SG + secret custom header.
S3 origin kept private → OAC.
Custom origin must use HTTPS → set origin protocol policy to HTTPS only.

questions.q: A company wants to serve a custom domain over HTTPS from CloudFront. The certificate was created in `eu-west-1`, and the browser shows a certificate error. What is the fix?

options.t: Request or import the ACM certificate in `us-east-1` and attach it, with the domain as an alternate domain name
options.why: Right: CloudFront only uses ACM certificates from us-east-1.
Wrong: CloudFront is a global service and has no Region.

options.t: Buy a dedicated IP custom SSL certificate
options.why: Wrong: it is a paid option for legacy clients and does not fix the Region.

options.t: Set the viewer protocol policy to HTTP and HTTPS
options.why: Wrong: it does not fix a certificate problem.

questions.explain: ACM certs for CloudFront live in us-east-1.
questions.remember: Certificate error on a CloudFront custom domain → cert not in us-east-1 or the CNAME (alternate domain name) is missing or not covered. WAF web ACLs for CloudFront are also created in us-east-1.
variants: Need all HTTP redirected → viewer protocol policy Redirect HTTP to HTTPS.
Legacy clients without SNI → dedicated IP SSL (paid).
Sensitive form fields → field-level encryption.

questions.q: Analysts need per-request CDN usage analytics at low cost, and a separate alert within seconds on abusive traffic. Which combination fits?

options.t: Standard logs to S3 queried with Athena, and real-time logs to Kinesis Data Streams for alerting
options.why: Right: standard logs are cheap and queryable; real-time logs arrive within seconds.

options.t: Real-time logs only, queried in Athena directly
options.why: Wrong: real-time logs go to Kinesis Data Streams, not straight to Athena.
Wrong: it records control-plane changes, not viewer requests.
Wrong: they give aggregates, not per-request fields.

questions.explain: Standard logs to S3 for analytics, real-time logs to Kinesis for seconds-level visibility.
questions.remember: Per-request analytics → standard logs to S3 + Athena (partition them). Second-level visibility → real-time logs to Kinesis Data Streams.
variants: Cache hit rate or origin latency graphs → additional CloudWatch metrics (extra cost).
Who changed the distribution → CloudTrail.
Delivery into OpenSearch or S3 from the stream → Kinesis Data Firehose.

questions.q: IoT clients far from the Region need a static pair of IP addresses and a TCP/UDP backend with health-based failover. Which service fits?

options.why: Right: it gives two static anycast IPs, supports TCP/UDP and fails over by endpoint health, with no caching.
Wrong: it is HTTP(S) and caches content, and fixed IPs are not its default.
Wrong: it only speeds up uploads to S3.
Wrong: it is DNS routing and does not give static anycast IPs.

questions.remember: TCP/UDP, fixed IPs, fast failover, no cache → Global Accelerator; HTTP(S) content with caching → CloudFront.
variants: Large uploads to S3 from far clients → S3 Transfer Acceleration.
Cache content at the edge → CloudFront.
Public API needing WAF and caching control → regional API Gateway plus your own CloudFront.

questions.q: An API must validate a JWT at the edge cheaply for millions of requests per second, with no network calls. Another API needs custom auth that calls an external service. Which choices fit? Choose 2.

options.t: CloudFront Functions for the JWT validation
options.why: Right: lightweight, sub-millisecond JavaScript at the viewer events, and cheaper than Lambda@Edge.

options.t: Lambda@Edge for the auth that calls an external service
options.why: Right: it can make network calls and use the AWS SDK; CloudFront Functions cannot.

options.t: CloudFront Functions for the external service call
options.why: Wrong: they have no network access.

options.t: Lambda@Edge for the JWT check at millions of requests per second
options.why: Wrong: it works, but costs more and scales to thousands of requests per second per Region.

questions.explain: Simple and cheap at the edge → CloudFront Functions; network calls or body access → Lambda@Edge.
questions.remember: Header rewrites, redirects, simple JWT checks, cache-key normalization → CloudFront Functions. Network calls, origin events, larger code → Lambda@Edge.
variants: Need origin request or response triggers → Lambda@Edge.
URL rewrite for index.html on a static site → CloudFront Function.
Need Python runtime → Lambda@Edge.
